hops.afterHeading: Adding inputs in time and in space
hops.title: Why a faint star fades when you look straight at it
hops.text: On a clear night, find a faint star and look straight at it. It often fades. Shift your gaze a little to one side and it comes back. The very center of the fovea has cones and no rods, so in light too dim for cones it leaves a blind patch about one degree across. Just off center, rods take over, and their signals converge: one model estimates that at peak about 53 rods feed through 4 rod bipolar cells and a single amacrine cell, relaying mostly via cone bipolar cells to 2 ganglion cells. Pooling many rods makes faint light easier to see, at the cost of fine detail.

sources.citation: Kalloniates M & Luu C, Light and Dark Adaptation, Webvision (University of Utah)
McKyton A, Elul D & Levin N, iScience 27(2):108929 (2024)
Dey A, Zele AJ, Feigl B & Adhikari P, Vision Research 180:1-10 (2021)

hops.afterHeading: When GABA pushes up: timing and site
hops.title: How nerve injury flips a spinal pain brake
hops.text: The potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 pumps chloride out of neurons, which helps inhibitory synapses keep them from firing. In 2003, Jeffrey Coull, Yves De Koninck and colleagues studied rats after a peripheral nerve injury. Neurons in lamina I of the spinal dorsal horn, one of the main routes carrying pain signals up to the brain, had reduced their KCC2 expression. With less chloride pumped out, the anion gradient shifted, and synaptic currents that normally inhibit these neurons became excitatory, driving their firing up. The team then blocked or knocked down spinal KCC2 in uninjured rats, and that change alone markedly lowered the threshold at which they showed a pain response.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white laboratory rat sitting calmly on a wire-mesh platform in a tidy lab room.
image.caption: In uninjured rats, blocking or reducing spinal KCC2 alone was enough to lower the threshold for a pain response.

hops.title: Filming a lobster's stomach teeth in two chewing modes
hops.text: Lobsters chew with three teeth inside the stomach, a middle one and two serrated side ones, driven by a circuit in the thirty-neuron stomatogastric ganglion. Cut off from their usual modulatory input in a lab dish, those neurons fall silent or fire steadily with no rhythm. In 1988, Hans-Georg Heinzel slipped an endoscope down the esophagus of restrained lobsters to film the teeth. A low dose of the neuromodulator proctolin in the circulation brought on squeeze mode, all three teeth pressing together. A higher dose brought on cut-and-grind mode, with the side teeth grinding backward along the middle one. One injection kept the chewing going for 2 to 30 minutes.

sources.citation: Selverston A et al., Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 860:35-50 (1998)

audio.title: A rejected paper, a goldfish brake and a lobster's stomach teeth
audio.transcript:
On paper, synaptic integration looks like tidy algebra: conductances, balance points, fractions. In real nervous systems the same rules have started an academic feud, steered a startled fish, and rearranged a lobster's dinner. Here are three stories.

First, the nineteen fifties. John Eccles and his colleagues were recording from spinal motor neurons. To interpret a brief voltage change, they treated each cell as if it had no dendrites. They had estimated the membrane resistivity about ten times too low. Because the length constant, lambda, depends on membrane resistivity, their lambda came out more than three times too short. That led them to conclude that synapses far out on the dendrites faded before reaching the cell body and were virtually ineffective. In nineteen fifty-eight, a biophysicist named Wilfrid Rall worked through the cable math for branching dendrites and sent a manuscript to the Journal of General Physiology arguing that dendrites matter. A referee's negative review persuaded the editors to reject it. As Rall later told it, the returned manuscript was so full of marginal notes that it was obvious the referee was Eccles himself. The editors of a brand-new journal, Experimental Neurology, then encouraged Rall to expand the work, and it appeared as two papers in nineteen fifty-nine and nineteen sixty. Over the following years his math held up, and distant dendritic synapses were shown to be effective after all.

Second, a goldfish. Every goldfish has a matched pair of giant neurons in its hindbrain called Mauthner cells, one on each side, and a spike in one of them can launch a fast escape turn away from a sudden sound. When researchers electrically stimulated the front branch of the lateral line nerve, the Mauthner cell on that side began to depolarize in about zero point eight milliseconds. About one millisecond after that, shunting inhibition arrived on top of the E P S P. Along the cell's lateral dendrite, the inhibitory release sites have odd horseshoe and ring shapes, a layout the authors think maximizes the shunt near excitatory inputs. In larval zebrafish, which have Mauthner cells too, recurrent inhibition and inhibition between the two partner cells also damp their responses. The same input reached the opposite Mauthner cell later and weaker, and the researchers proposed that this difference helps decide which cell fires, and so which way the fish turns.

Finally, a lobster. Lobsters chew with three teeth inside the stomach, driven by a circuit in a ganglion of about thirty neurons, the stomatogastric ganglion. Cut off from their usual modulatory input in a lab dish, those neurons fall quiet or fire steadily with no rhythm. In nineteen eighty-eight, Hans-Georg Heinzel slid a small endoscope down a lobster's esophagus and filmed the teeth at work. A low dose of the neuromodulator proctolin, injected into the circulation, put all three teeth into what he called squeeze mode, pressing together. A higher dose brought on cut-and-grind mode instead, with the side teeth grinding backward along the middle tooth. A single injection kept the lobster chewing for anywhere from two to thirty minutes.

Three animals, one set of rules: how far a signal spreads along a dendrite, how an open conductance can clamp it, and how a chemical in the blood can change the ropes themselves.
